section.title: The Decree of Cyrus
section.sectionRationale: The book opens by answering a question the exile had left hanging: is God's word finished, or will He keep His promise to bring His people home? In the first year of Cyrus the LORD moves a pagan emperor to release the exiles and fund the rebuilding of His house, and He restores the very vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off. It is one movement: the word of God, the stirred king, the willing people, and the returned treasures.
section.thesis: God keeps His word by ruling the heart of a Persian king, stirring the spirits of His people, and restoring true worship, so that the return from exile begins not with human strength but with the sovereign, faithful hand of God.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the LORD stirs Cyrus to decree the return, verses 1 to 4; the family heads and priests are stirred to go up, verses 5 and 6; and the holy vessels are counted out and carried back to Jerusalem, verses 7 to 11.

units.label: The LORD stirs Cyrus to decree the return
units.note: to fulfill the word of the LORD

verses.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD {{uwr|stirred}} the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows:
“This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah.
Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem.

And let every {{sheerit|survivor}}, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a {{nedabah|freewill offering}} for the house of God in Jerusalem.’”

units.label: The people are stirred to go up
units.note: everyone whose spirit God had stirred

verses.text: So the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred, prepared to go up and rebuild the {{bayit|house}} of the LORD in Jerusalem.
And all their neighbors supported them with articles of silver and gold, with goods and livestock, and with valuables, in addition to all their freewill offerings.
King Cyrus also brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods.
Cyrus king of Persia had them brought out by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.
This was the inventory: 30 gold dishes, 1,000 silver dishes, 29 silver utensils,
30 gold bowls, 410 matching silver bowls, and 1,000 other articles.
In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles. Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

uwr.gloss: To rouse, awaken, or stir up. The same verb frames the whole chapter: the LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus in verse 1 and stirs the spirits of His people in verse 5. God does not merely predict the return; He inwardly moves both a pagan king and His own people to accomplish it.

sheerit.gloss: One who is left, a survivor or remnant. Those who return are the leftover ones, the surviving remnant of a nation that had been all but swept away. The word carries the hope that runs through the prophets: God always preserves a remnant through judgment.

nedabah.gloss: A freewill offering, a gift given willingly rather than commanded. The return and the rebuilding are funded by glad, uncoerced giving, an early mark of hearts that God Himself has stirred to seek His house.

bayit.gloss: House, and here the house of the LORD, the temple. The whole book turns on this bayit: God's dwelling among His people. Its rebuilding points beyond stone to the true temple, Christ, and to the church He indwells by His Spirit.

basic.context: The book of Ezra opens about fifty years after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and carried Judah into exile. Jeremiah had promised the captivity would last seventy years and then end. Here, in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, God keeps that promise: He moves Cyrus to issue a decree letting the exiles go home and rebuild the temple, and He even returns the sacred vessels Nebuchadnezzar had stolen. The key question is simple: who is really running this? The answer is God.
basic.hermeneutics: This is history, and it is told to show God's hand behind world events. Cyrus was a real emperor with his own political reasons for his policy, yet the text says the LORD stirred his spirit to fulfill the word spoken through Jeremiah. We should read the decree as fulfilled prophecy, not as a model for how to run governments. The abiding truth is that God keeps His promises and rules the hearts of kings.
basic.originalLanguages: One verb ties the chapter together: God stirred, ur, the spirit of Cyrus, and He stirred the spirits of His people. Those who come home are the survivors, the remnant. And they give freewill offerings, nedabah, gladly, toward the house, the bayit, of the LORD.
basic.typology: The return from exile is a picture of a greater homecoming. The temple being rebuilt points forward to Christ, the true temple, and to the church. The stirring of a pagan king to serve God's people foreshadows the day when the nations bring their glory into the city of God.
basic.christ: God moved an unbelieving emperor to release His people and restore true worship. In the same way, God works through all of history, even through those who do not know Him, to bring about the redemption that comes to a head in Jesus. The little return under Cyrus is a down payment on the great return from the exile of sin that Christ accomplishes.
basic.god: God is sovereign and faithful. He rules the most powerful ruler on earth as easily as a stream of water, and He keeps the promise He made through Jeremiah down to the year. He is also the God who stirs hearts, moving people from the inside to seek Him.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 29:10 promised seventy years and then a return. Isaiah 44:28 named Cyrus by name long before he was born. 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 tells the same decree. And Proverbs 21:1 says the king's heart is a stream the LORD turns wherever He wills.
basic.oneStory: The exile was the low point of Israel's story, and it looked like the promises had failed. Chapter one is God saying no: His word stands. He brings a remnant home to rebuild His house, and that homecoming is a small, true picture of the great homecoming He will accomplish in Christ.

context.literary:
The chapter is built in three short scenes, each pivoting on the same verb: the LORD stirs Cyrus to speak, verse 1; the LORD stirs the people's own spirits to respond, verse 5; and the treasurer effectively stirs a much older story back into motion by counting out the temple's own vessels into Sheshbazzar's hands, verses 7 to 11. The verb frames the whole unit like a set of bookends, so that a king's public proclamation and a leader's private register are shown to spring from exactly the same divine cause.

Ezra's opening two verses are also a deliberate literary seam. They repeat, almost word for word, the closing two verses of 2 Chronicles, 36:22-23, a technique ancient scribes used to join two originally separate scrolls into one continuous account, called resumptive repetition. A reader moving from the last scroll of the Hebrew Bible in its traditional order to the first scroll of a new one is meant to feel no seam at all, only one sentence carrying straight across the break.

The precise inventory that closes the chapter, an exact count of gold dishes, silver dishes, bowls, and other articles down to the last unit, is a genre this book returns to often, most fully in the long roll call of chapter 2. Numbers here are never filler; they are the narrator's proof that a specific, countable, verifiable people and a specific, countable, verifiable set of vessels really did go home.
context.historical:
Cyrus took Babylon without a lengthy siege in 539 BC, entering a city whose own king, Nabonidus, had left the capital in the hands of his son Belshazzar for the sake of a long stay at Tema, a background the book of Daniel narrates from the inside on the very night the city fell, Daniel 5. The first year of Cyrus in Ezra's opening line counts from that conquest, not from decades earlier when Cyrus had already been reigning as a Persian king in his own right, so the decree belongs to his very first year ruling the empire he had just inherited from Babylon.

A famous inscription from this same period, the cylinder Cyrus had buried in Babylon's own foundations, records a policy of returning displaced peoples to their homelands and restoring the worship of their own gods, a broader pattern into which Judah's return fits, even though Ezra's version of the decree is framed entirely in terms of the LORD, the God of Israel, rather than the language of Cyrus's own religion.

Sheshbazzar, called the prince of Judah, is generally taken to be a member of the royal Davidic line, perhaps the Shenazzar listed among the sons of Jeconiah in 1 Chronicles 3:18, entrusted with the first, official leadership of the return before Zerubbabel takes on the fuller role Ezra 3 to 5 describe.
context.canonical:
Ezra 1 opens the whole run of literature the Old Testament devotes to the postexilic community, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and every one of those books assumes the decree recorded here as its starting point. The chapter's insistence that this happened to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, verse 1, is itself a formula the New Testament uses constantly of Jesus, joining this return to a whole pattern of Scripture proving itself reliable across centuries.

The return is also deliberately shaped as a new exodus. Israel's neighbors supply the departing exiles with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, verse 6, echoing how the Egyptians, plundered, sent Israel out with silver, gold, and clothing at the first exodus, Exodus 12:35-36. Both departures are funded, in the end, by the very people who had held Israel captive, and both are described as Israel going up, the same verb used of the exodus itself, Exodus 3:8.

Isaiah's naming of Cyrus more than a century before his birth, Isaiah 44:28, remains one of the most striking predictive statements in the Old Testament, specific enough that some later readers have questioned whether it must have been written after the fact; the text itself, however, presents it as spoken well in advance precisely so that Cyrus, and everyone else, would know that I am the LORD, who calls you by name, Isaiah 45:3-4, a purpose that only works if the naming truly came first.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants his exiled and returning readers to know, in the plainest possible terms, that this moment did not originate in Persian politics but in the mouth of God spoken generations earlier through Jeremiah. Naming Cyrus's motive as the LORD stirring his spirit, rather than merely reporting the decree's contents, is itself a theological claim laid over a political event, telling the reader how to read every decree, every census, and every gift of silver and gold that follows in this book.

He also wants to root the identity of the returning community in willing response rather than compulsion. The same stirring that moves an emperor moves ordinary family heads to volunteer, verse 5, so that the whole community reading this account, whether they themselves went up in that first company or were among the many who stayed in Babylon, could recognize their own possible response mirrored in it: God does not merely announce that a way home exists; God moves people to walk it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates one particular, unrepeatable act of God working through one particular emperor at one particular turning point in redemptive history; it is not a pattern that guarantees believers can expect a government to fund their worship, nor a promise that every exile ends within a set number of years merely because this one did.

What endures is the theology beneath the history: that God's sovereignty over rulers is real even when those rulers never learn his name, that the stirring of a heart to serve him is his own gift rather than an achievement, and that a fixed prophetic word, however long it takes, arrives on schedule. Applied today, the chapter teaches believers to expect God's providence to work through ordinary political events rather than only through visibly religious ones, and to respond to whatever stirring they sense in themselves the way these family heads did, by rising up rather than waiting to be forced.

debates.question: In what sense did the LORD stir the spirit of Cyrus?

views.label: Through Cyrus's own political and religious reasoning
views.case: Cyrus's own inscriptions credit Marduk, Babylon's god, for his rise and describe him restoring other nations' gods and peoples to their homes; a reader can hold that God worked through these very motives and habits of Persian policy without Cyrus perceiving any conflict between serving his own gods and unknowingly serving the LORD.

views.label: Through a direct, effective act on the king's own will
views.case: The text names the LORD, not policy, as the acting cause, and Proverbs 21:1 states as a general principle that the king's heart is a stream of water in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he wills, suggesting the stirring here is one instance of a truth true of every throne.

debates.bearing: Both readings uphold the main point: the decree was ultimately God's act, not merely Persian policy, which is why the exiles could trust that the God who began the return would see it through.

debates.question: Was Cyrus a true believer in the LORD?

views.label: A pagan king used by God
views.case: Cyrus honored many gods and speaks of the LORD as one deity among the peoples he served; his confession is diplomatic, and Isaiah 45:4-5 says God calls him by name though he does not know him.

views.label: A king given real, if limited, light
views.case: His words in verses 2 and 3 confess the LORD as the God of heaven who gave him his kingdoms and appointed him to build the temple, which sounds like genuine, though limited, acknowledgment rather than mere diplomatic language.

debates.bearing: Either way the lesson holds: God can accomplish the good of his people through rulers who do not fully know him, so his purposes never depend on the faith of kings.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words carry unusual weight in this short chapter. The verb behind stirred, ur, means literally to rouse from sleep or to wake. Isaiah uses the identical imperative twice to summon Zion herself to respond to her own deliverance, awake, awake, Isaiah 51:9 and 52:1, so that the same verb which describes God rousing an emperor in this chapter had already been used to describe God calling his own people to rouse themselves, a hint that the stirring in verse 5 is not one-directional: God wakes the king, and God wakes the exiles to walk through the door that waking opens.

The survivors, sheerit, share their root, shaar, to remain, with one of Isaiah's most famous prophetic signs. Isaiah names his own son Shear-jashub, a remnant will return, Isaiah 7:3, more than a century before this chapter, so that the very word used here for who returns had already been spoken as a living prophecy attached to a child's name.

The freewill offering, nedabah, from nadab, to volunteer, describes exactly the kind of giving Israel had already been asked for once before, when Moses called for a nedabah to build the first tabernacle and the people gave more than enough, Exodus 35:29 and 36:3-7. The same word for the same kind of uncoerced generosity funds the rebuilding of a house their own great grandparents had once furnished the same way.

Finally, bayit, house, carries a double meaning the chapter quietly leans on. God had told David centuries earlier that David would not build God a bayit, a temple, but that God would instead build David a bayit, a dynasty, 2 Samuel 7:11-13. Here the physical bayit is finally being rebuilt while the dynastic bayit, the line of David, sits without a king on any throne, a silence this chapter does not explain but that the rest of Scripture eventually answers in the son of David who is himself the true and final bayit where God dwells with his people.

The same word for spirit, ruach, also names the wind and the breath, the animating force behind creation itself, Genesis 1:2, and behind every living thing, Genesis 6:17. When this ruach is stirred in Cyrus and again in the family heads of verse 5, the chapter borrows the vocabulary of life itself for what looks, on the surface, like nothing more than a political decree and a change of address.

typology.type: The remnant named and gathered before it ever returns
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah had already given a remnant, sheerit, a name and a promise a century before any exile began, Shear-jashub, Isaiah 7:3, and this chapter shows exactly that promised remnant beginning to walk home. Paul later applies the same principle to his own generation, there is at the present time a remnant chosen by grace, Romans 11:5, so that the pattern of a preserved minority carrying God's larger purpose forward through judgment becomes, in Christ, the pattern of how God saves at every point in history, never the whole nation at once, always a remnant first.

typology.type: A house rebuilt while a promised dynasty still waits
typology.fulfillment: God had promised David two things by the same word, bayit, a temple God's people would build for him and a dynasty God himself would build for David, 2 Samuel 7:11-13. Cyrus's decree restores only the first, a house of stone with no king of David's line to fill it. The second half of that promise waits four centuries longer, until an angel tells Mary that the Lord God will give her son the throne of his father David, Luke 1:32, joining the two houses back together in one person.

typology.type: Plundered captors funding their former captives' worship
typology.fulfillment: Israel's neighbors supply silver, gold, goods, and livestock to the departing exiles, verse 6, the same shape as Egypt's own people giving Israel silver, gold, and clothing on the night of the first exodus, Exodus 12:35-36. Both scenes show the nations that once profited from Israel's bondage sending them out enriched rather than empty handed, a pattern Isaiah later expands into a picture of the nations bringing their own wealth into the city of God, Isaiah 60:5-11.

typology.type: A pagan decree issued to build God's house
typology.fulfillment: Cyrus announces that God has appointed him to build a house for him at Jerusalem, verse 2, unknowingly stepping into a commission God had first given Solomon, 1 Kings 5:5. What one king begins by force of empire, another far greater son of David will finish not with stone but by building his own people into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5, so that Cyrus's brick and timber anticipate a temple made of living people.

study.christ:
This chapter's whole momentum rests on a single, striking claim: an emperor with no covenant relationship to Israel's God becomes the means by which God's ancient promise through Jeremiah is kept to the year. That same pattern reappears, deliberately widened, when God moves an entirely different pagan ruler to issue a census that puts a pregnant woman on the road to Bethlehem at exactly the moment prophecy required, so that Caesar Augustus, like Cyrus, serves a purpose he never intended and never perceived, Luke 2:1-7 and Micah 5:2. The empire that does not know the God of Israel becomes, twice over centuries apart, the unwitting instrument of his most important promises being kept.

The return itself is also a small rehearsal of a far larger homecoming. Jesus opens his own ministry by reading from Isaiah's promise of release for the captives, Luke 4:18, and later applies exile language directly to spiritual bondage, everyone who sins is a slave to sin, John 8:34, so that everyone still living under sin's rule is, in the terms this book already understands, an exile waiting for a decree of release. Christ's death and resurrection function as that greater Cyrus moment, a sovereign act that opens the way home once for all rather than merely once, for one specific captivity, at one specific point in history.

The chapter's freewill giving anticipates the New Testament's own instruction to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, but because God loves a cheerful giver, 2 Corinthians 9:7, the same posture Israel's family heads show here centuries earlier. And the vessels restored to the house of the LORD, taken by force and now returned intact down to the last item, quietly picture what Christ does with everything sin has stolen: nothing precious to God is lost forever, even what an enemy has carried off for decades, because the God who counts every gold dish by name will not leave what belongs to him permanently in a foreign temple.
study.god:
God's sovereignty in this chapter operates on two very different registers at once, and the text refuses to let either one eclipse the other. On one register he moves the most powerful man on earth, an emperor who has just inherited the largest empire the world had yet seen, as easily and as invisibly as stirring a sleeper awake. On the other register he moves ordinary, unnamed family heads in the same verse's structure, verse 5, using the identical verb, so that the reader is meant to see no difference in kind between God ruling Cyrus's throne and God moving an Israelite father to sell his house and go.

His faithfulness is exact rather than approximate. Jeremiah had said seventy years, and the narrative marks this decree as coming in the first year of Cyrus to fulfill that very word, verse 1, a note of precision the chronicler had already sounded once at the end of the previous book, 2 Chronicles 36:21-22. God's promises are not treated here as broad tendencies that eventually work out; they are treated as appointments kept on a calendar only he controls.

God's holiness and mercy meet in what he restores and what he still withholds. He restores the sacred vessels down to the smallest article, verses 7 to 11, proof that his own house and its worship still matter to him after decades of apparent silence, yet he restores a diminished nation to a still subject province rather than an independent throne, so that even this generous act of mercy carries a visible reminder that judgment has consequences a single decree does not erase.

Above all, this is a God who works from the inside. Cyrus is not merely permitted or commanded; his spirit is stirred. The family heads are not merely informed of an opportunity; their spirits are stirred as well. Scripture elsewhere calls this same inward movement writing God's law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, so that Ezra 1 shows, in miniature and well before that new covenant fully arrives, exactly what it looks like when God moves people to obey him from the inside rather than merely commanding them from the outside.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah's letter to the first wave of exiles promises that after seventy years God will fulfill his good word and bring them back to this place. Ezra 1:1 opens by naming this exact promise as what Cyrus's decree fulfills, tying a private pastoral letter written decades earlier directly to a public imperial edict.

Isaiah names Cyrus by name and calls him God's shepherd and anointed more than a century before his birth, promising in Cyrus's own voice that Jerusalem would be rebuilt and the temple's foundation laid. Ezra 1 opens with precisely that rebuilding beginning to happen.

The king's heart is like channels of water in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he pleases. Cyrus's own decree, issued as though entirely his own idea, becomes in this proverb's terms one more channel God has simply directed toward Jerusalem.

The closing verses of Chronicles repeat this decree almost word for word, deliberately overlapping the two books at exactly this point so that the reader passes from one scroll to the next without any sense of a gap in the story.

Isaiah names his own son Shear-jashub, a remnant will return, generations before any of this chapter's survivors are born, embedding the promise of a returning remnant into a living child's name long before there was any exile for a remnant to return from.

The Israelites leaving Egypt receive silver, gold, and clothing from the very Egyptians who had enslaved them. The exiles leaving Babylon receive silver, gold, goods, and livestock from their neighbors in the same way, Ezra 1:6, so that the return is deliberately patterned after the first exodus.

God promises David that David will not build God a house, but that God will build David a house, a dynasty. Cyrus's decree rebuilds the physical house God's people build for him, while the dynastic house God promised to build for David still waits, at this point in the story, for its promised heir.

Israel had already been asked once before for a freewill offering, and had given more than enough to build the first tabernacle. The same word for the same kind of uncoerced generosity appears again here, funding a second house their ancestors had also helped to furnish.

Paul calls the believing minority in his own day a remnant chosen by grace, the same principle this chapter shows in miniature: God has never saved an entire generation at once, only ever a preserved remnant carrying his purpose forward.

Peter describes believers themselves as living stones being built into a spiritual house. Cyrus authorizes a house of stone and timber for God in Jerusalem; the New Testament describes an even greater house, made of people, still being built today.

study.oneStory:
Exile had looked, for two full generations, like the end of everything God had promised Israel. The line of David sat in Babylon rather than on a throne, the temple lay in ashes, and the land that once flowed with milk and honey had been left to the foxes. Ezra 1 answers that despair directly, not with an argument, but with a decree, issued in exactly the year and through exactly the means Jeremiah had said it would come.

This chapter sits at the hinge between judgment completed and restoration beginning, the same hinge every return narrative in Scripture eventually rests on. Just as God once moved Pharaoh's own household through plagues to send Israel out of Egypt with plunder in hand, he now stirs a foreign emperor's own spirit to send Israel out of Babylon the same way, so that the second exodus, like the first, begins with someone outside the covenant unknowingly serving the God who chose Israel.

But this return is modest by design, a shrunken remnant, a still subject province, a house rebuilt smaller than the one Solomon had raised. It is not the full and final homecoming Isaiah and Jeremiah had also promised, only its first real installment, and the very line of kings Cyrus's decree cannot yet restore is still waiting, generations later, for the true Son of David who will gather a far larger remnant than any single decree could send home. What Cyrus opens with an edict, Christ opens with an empty tomb, the greater exile of sin and death giving way at last to a homecoming with no need of any further decree, since the one who leads it also built the house himself.

quiz.q: Why does the text say Cyrus issued his decree?

options.text: Because the LORD stirred his spirit, to fulfill the word spoken through Jeremiah.
options.note: Verse 1 gives God's action and the fulfillment of prophecy as the true cause.

options.text: Because it was standard Persian policy to send peoples home.
options.note: Persian policy was the human means, but the text names God's stirring as the deeper reason.

options.text: Because the exiles had grown powerful enough to demand it.
options.note: The exiles were a small remnant with no power to demand anything.

options.text: Because Cyrus had become a devout worshiper of the LORD alone.
options.note: Isaiah 45:4-5 says God used Cyrus though he did not truly know Him.

quiz.q: What promise was being fulfilled in this chapter?

options.text: Jeremiah's word that after seventy years in Babylon God would bring His people home.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly links the decree to the word through Jeremiah, see Jeremiah 29:10.

options.text: The promise that Israel would never again be conquered.
options.note: No such promise is in view; the point is the promised return after exile.

options.text: A promise made by Cyrus to his own gods.
options.note: The fulfilled word is God's promise through Jeremiah, not a Persian vow.

options.text: There was no prior promise; this was simply good fortune.
options.note: The text roots the event in God's prophetic word, not chance.

quiz.q: What does the repeated word stirred tell us about the return?

options.text: God moved both the king and His people from within, so the return was His work in every part.
options.note: The verb ur is used of Cyrus in verse 1 and the people in verse 5.

options.text: The people worked up their own enthusiasm to go home.
options.note: Human willingness was real, but the text credits God's stirring as its source.

options.text: Only Cyrus was moved; the people were forced to go.
options.note: The people went willingly, their spirits also stirred by God.

options.text: It tells us nothing in particular; it is just narration.
options.note: The deliberate repetition makes God's inward working the theme of the chapter.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter carefully inventory the temple vessels?

options.text: To show God restoring true worship, returning the very articles Nebuchadnezzar had stolen.
options.note: The counted vessels signal the recovery of the LORD's house and worship.

options.text: To prove the exiles were wealthy.
options.note: The vessels belong to the LORD's house, not to private wealth; the point is restored worship.

options.text: To record a business transaction with no deeper meaning.
options.note: The careful count underscores God's faithful restoration, not mere bookkeeping.

options.text: To show the exiles had made new idols.
options.note: These are the holy vessels of the LORD, being restored, not idols.

quiz.q: How does the decree of Cyrus point us toward Christ?

options.text: God rules even unbelieving rulers to free His people and restore worship, as He does supremely in the redemption Christ brings.
options.note: The return foreshadows the greater deliverance and the true temple in Jesus.

options.text: It shows that political power is the way God saves.
options.note: God uses rulers, but salvation comes through Christ, not political power itself.

options.text: It teaches that only kings can do God's work.
options.note: God stirs kings and ordinary people alike; the work is His.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ or the gospel.
options.note: The return from exile is a key thread that runs to Christ's greater rescue.

questions: God kept His word through Jeremiah down to the year, even when the exile looked final. Where do you need to trust that a promise of God still stands, though circumstances say otherwise?
The LORD turned the heart of the most powerful man on earth to serve His people. How does God's rule over rulers steady you when you look at the leaders and headlines of your own day?
God stirred the spirits of ordinary family heads to rise up and rebuild. Where might God be stirring you to give yourself to His work, and what is your response?
The exiles gave freewill offerings gladly toward the house of God. What would glad, uncoerced generosity toward God's work look like in your life right now?
The return from exile is a small picture of the great homecoming Christ secures. How does knowing your true home is guaranteed in Jesus change the way you live as an exile here?

translationNotes.note: To fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah refers to the seventy-year prophecy of Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10; the same verb rendered stirred is used again in verse 5 of the people.

Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah leads the first return; the BSB footnote explains the phrase means the leader of the exiles returning to Judah. He is later distinguished in the narrative from Zerubbabel.
The numbers and terms for the dishes and utensils are technical and slightly uncertain in the Hebrew; the totals are given to stress the full restoration of the LORD's holy vessels.
